📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that how do you make the The Tired Dad perk up? Get vulnerable.

Jon Gustin is tired. But he's not complaining. To the contrary, Gustin, better known as The Tired Dad, holds up his fatigue as a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.” Tiredness is his brand, sure, but it’s also a conversation starter — a way to assess and unpack the strain that kids, relationships, work, and showing up for your family can put on you.

Gustin’s social feed is something of a sacred space. There’s a melancholy confessional aspect to it, in which he offers statements like, “I’m constantly thinking about what I’m leaving behind…” Yes, it’s a familiar sentiment, but one that we rarely dare to face straight-on. In this sense, The Tired Dad feels nearly dystopian, like Gustin is playing the role of the protagonist in Lois Lowry’s The Giver, the Receiver of Memory who takes on the pains that those in society do not face. But then, out of darkness, there is Gustin as motivational speaker, coach, and teacher. In facing the darkness, he finds the light. He ends most posts with a mantra such as, “Keep showing up.”.

It has been revealed that gustin has taken his social media philosophizing and translated it to a book, The Tired Dad: 100 Reflections on Showing Up for What Matters Most, out now. Inside, you’ll find fleshed-out contemplations and personal histories and, of course, plenty of advice on being a man, sobriety, marriage, fatherhood, and vulnerability.

In a recent development, just a week out from his book release, I had the chance to talk with Gustin. He didn’t come ready to push his book — with the influencer energy you might expect — but with his signature sincerity that, I realized, is part of his practice. "Vulnerability is freedom," Gustin tells me shortly into our discussion. "And not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone." Here, to help us all feel a little less alone, is our full conversation.

This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

It has been revealed that jon Gustin: I like to bring up the fact that my dad entered the Marine Corps at the ripe age of 17. His parents had to sign for him and he was in Vietnam by the time he was 18 and he spent just over two years there. It's hard to wrap my mind around that.

In a recent development, the number one thing he's taught me is character. And he learned that from his dad, who was in World War II in the Navy. I come from a very military background, very structured, and with men that don’t show much emotion. I think I've seen my dad cry about five times, and three in maybe the past couple years. But he always taught me about character, saying stuff like, "If you say you're going to do something, do it." True character is when no one's looking, you always do the right thing. And not only did my dad and grandpa say that stuff, they showed it every single day in their actions. If he said he was going to play catch with me or go to something, he would make it happen. So that's kind of my dad in a nutshell.

Industry observers note that in the book, it’s clear you held your grandfather in great esteem. Tell me about him as a role model.

When I was writing this book, my grandfather passed away, at the age of 99. And that passage I wrote in the book was right after he passed. Towards the end of his life, he was so unfiltered, but in a good way. He almost got more emotional and more expressive because I don't think he had that shield up anymore. And it was just kind of, he didn't care. And the way he talked about my grandmother and their marriage and just how much they loved each other is like a storybook.

In a recent development, my whole life, my grandfather was just a man of wisdom. He knew so much. He read the newspaper every day. He would read two books in a day. It was insane. So he was just full of wisdom and insight. And he didn't care about the stupid stuff in life, like the material things. It was always strictly like, who you are as a man, like truly, who are you?

According to recent reports, there's so many moments with my grandfather and the way he was. It was a different generation. So not too much expressive emotion there, but very, very kind. He always treated people so well. He was always there for us. They bought a motor home after retirement and they traveled everywhere to see all the grandkids and the great-grandkids and the whole family. And that's how they spent their money and their time. And they spent their money helping people out with donations. They would get audited all the time because they donated so much of their money that the government didn't believe in them. So that's who they were.

I'm wondering what you think of those men out there who have not had such role models. Absenteeism is a stubborn problem in this country ...

Sources indicate that I think fathers are such a vital, vital role in the dynamic of family. But even with the absenteeism, I know some fellow friends and stuff that had horrible relationships with their father or didn't have them at all, but they are the greatest fathers themselves. And they really are using that as motivation to just put their foot down and break that curse and to show up for the first time in their family — to be that shift in generational trauma, I guess. And it's weird to view myself as a role model just because I'm not perfect and I have made so many mistakes in my life early on, but I think I do want to be.

According to recent reports, as I say in the book, vulnerability is freedom and not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone. If you can express yourself, then other dads, other people will say, "Oh, I thought I was alone in that. But this person's expressing that. I must not be crazy." And it kind of frees them up. So if anything, I want to be just a role model to be vulnerable in your story and that we don't always have it figured out and that the point is not to figure it all out. The point is to be on a journey forever and to always be progressing towards something and to lead with wisdom and intentionality to be role models to your kids and as a side effect, to be a role model to others.

Vulnerability is at the core of what you put out there. Given that, I wonder what you think of stoicism. It's historically seen as a masculine trait and while is has been vilified for the repression of emotion, it seems to be getting a second look, especially with so many kids struggling with independence, perseverance, and resilience. I'm curious as to what you think about it and when to go vulnerable and when to go Stoic.

I sat down with Ryan Holiday not too long ago and I've always read his stuff. And before I kind of knew Ryan Holiday and his message of stoicism, the modern message of stoicism, I did just think it was this overly masculine thing — like, we are statues, we're Greek Gods who must keep chipping away. And it wasn't until I started to really dive into it and learn that, at least what Ryan preaches, that there is vulnerability in stoicism. Perseverance is great, but I still think there's an aspect of saying, "Hey, you know what? I'm defeated and I don't know." It’s okay if you don't have the answers. I think men want to fix everything and have the answers and they feel like they're dumb or they are weak if they don't have the answers. And I think that vulnerability of saying, "I don't have the answers.".

Recent findings suggest that and there's some extremes to stoicism. When the world is gladiator brutal, when Marcus Aurelius put his kids to bed every night as if he's never going to see them again. I don't think it's healthy to have that extreme a mentality. The whole memento mori, I wrote about it in the book — I want to think about it a little differently. I don't want to think about dying all the time. Sometimes I want to think about dying at 100 and living like I'm going to live to 100 because as I stated in the book, if you told me I was going to die tomorrow, yes, I would live my day today a lot differently, but chances are I'm probably not going to die tomorrow. I think men want this black and white way of thinking, and sometimes it's just not that way.

It has been revealed that and that's, again, men want to have this identity, right? Warrior, Spartan, Stoic, man. We want to be part of this group. I listen to Joe Rogan. I do jiu-jitsu. I do cold plunges, which I do all of those, but it's not my entire identity. Sometimes it can be your identity masking your true identity, your insecurities, your ego and everything like that.

Speaking to those extremes and that black and white thinking, what do you make of the more extreme corners of the manosphere?

I mean, the manosphere is birthed from insecurity. It's birthed from lack of identity. I speak from experience because in my early 20s ... I guess I was part of the manosphere before it was called that. I thought, I'm going to be a man. I'm going to view myself very highly and I'm going to be egotistical, but think I'm being manly. And there were mentors in my life too that were like that.

It has been revealed that and that I saw these men that were just powerful, but they were something, there was a red flag that I was like, they seem so insecure. Seem like they're overcompensating for something. And then they don't seem like they're like the greatest of husbands. And I was young, I was in my 20s so, but I could see so easily how impressionable young men can be on this manosphere type mentality because they're just looking for identity and they're so insecure and they really don't know how to talk to girls.

So if they just view girls as less than, then they can have power over them. And if they just become successful with money, then they can have power over people and there's no substance to it, but it's a search for identity of what masculinity is. And when you see this facade of masculinity, these guys with deep voices that talk real loud and are on steroids and it could like, okay, yeah, that's what I want.

Industry observers note that I look back on it, the things I valued as early 20s and now 20 years later, I mean, it's not even close. I'm like, "That's not what I value at all." Now, I value time and that's the greatest currency. Money is important clearly to an extent, but the obsession with money is empty and there's no cars that are going to fulfill you. There's no amount of women that's going to fulfill you. Actually, it does the opposite. And until you see that for yourself and other people or maybe experience it yourself, you realize that, yeah, this isn't masculine at all. This is weakness because, you're actually very weak and you’re overcompensating for all your insecurities.

Growth is hard. Do you see yourself as an expert in parenting, masculinity, relationships?

No, I'm not an expert in any of it. Expert is a funny word. To call yourself an expert makes you feel like you've reached the end. And I don't believe that there is an end until the end of there's always something to learn, there's always something to get better at. There's always something fresh to read. There's always more information. There's always something. So no, I don't consider myself an expert at all. I'm learning as I go.

Relationships get hard when you have kids. I think that's a fact of life and something you address a lot. For those newly introducing kids to their marriage, where can they start when the going gets hard?

Industry observers note that kids changed marriage completely. There are a lot of curve-balls there, but communication is huge. Kill your ego. Ego serves absolutely no purpose in a relationship. Meet the other person where they are, rather than trying to fix them. The other person's not going to fix themselves for you. You're going to fix yourself for the other person. Both of you fix yourselves to meet the other person, right, and to accept the other person and to work with the other person as teammates, not as competitors, because in competition you'll lose. It's just a lose-lose. Nobody wins in that.

Sources indicate that so I think it's effective communication, vulnerable communication. Because it's not just communicating — just complaining about the other person, that's not effective communication. Effective communication is where the other person doesn't get defensive. You're not attacking them. You're trying to solve a problem. And once you kill your ego and stop being so defensive to everything, you guys can start communicating in an effective way, and then that's where the growth happens.

I see these days more men on the playgrounds, more men parenting in public spaces. But I still don’t see, well, full participation in parenting. I'm part of the PTA, for example, and am often the only dad in the room. Sometimes I go to the pediatrician and am the only dad taking my kids there. What would you like to push men to do more of?

According to recent reports, well, just to get out of that idea that your only job is a financial provider. You work and when you're done with work, you're done with work. I want fathers to view their role as a dad just as key, probably more important than their work job, than their job title. When you come home, you need to put on your other cap, which is dad, and that's your most important role. So the work doesn't stop. It's why we're so tired because the work never stops.

My wife and I are transplants. I'm from California. She's from Ohio, and we met in Tennessee and started our family here. Nobody around, no village per se. And I think sometimes it was so hard that I got resentful of other people who had helpful grandparents nearby.

According to recent reports, but now I look back on it and realize it made me a better dad to force myself to wake up so early in the morning and then come home and watch my kids and then go back to work and play this tag team with my wife. It was draining and hard, but now I look at it as kind of a blessing. Because first of all, I have a ton of memories with my kids growing up. I think my kids will think I was with them 24/7 because I am with them so much. There are times when, okay, I'm canceling my clients. I'm losing money today because my kid is sick. I got to take him to the pediatrician. My wife can't take off work. It is what it is. And that's just made me so much of a better dad.

And that's the badge of honor of a tired dad, that we wear because we're showing up in all areas. We are showing up to work, but we're showing up until we put our heads down.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a plant that’s such an iconic part of our festive decorations, the Christmas cactus is surprisingly sensitive when it comes to flowering well. Put this beloved houseplant in the wrong spot in your home and its flowerbuds could even drop off – yes, every last precious one! So, it pays to know what conditions will keep your Christmas cactus happy, and the common spots that will likely lead to a dramatic bud drop and zero holiday blooms.

Industry observers note that when we think of cacti, most of us naturally picture a dry desert environment baking under a scorching sun. But Christmas cacti evolved to live in the rainforests of Brazil, where they thrive in damp air and dappled sunlight. They don’t grow in soil in the ground but cling to tree branches or shady rock crevices, their roots anchored in small pockets of decomposing leaves. And that’s a far cry from living in a pot of soil in the dry air of our well-heated homes – which is why Shlumbergera can be so persnickety about the conditions they require to flower well.

Recent findings suggest that once you appreciate why your plant is so fussy, it’s easy to give a Christmas cactus everything it needs in November and December to swell its buds into bounteous blooms. And if you’ve gone to the effort of persuading a Christmas cactus to bloom right on time for the holidays, don't waste all your hard work by putting your plant in the wrong spot now! For a glorious cascade of flowering stems to add to your holiday decor, these are the five spots to avoid.

It has been revealed that developing buds and blooms require a tremendous amount of energy, and a Christmas cactus gets 100% of this from sunlight. While Shlumbergera needs regular periods of dark to set its buds, as soon as you spot those tiny dots of color on the stem ends, the plant needs to be moved to get more light, otherwise it won’t have enough energy to develop them into flowers.

The type of light is crucial, too. Because Christmas cacti naturally live in a rainforest under a canopy of leaves, indirect sunlight is best. That simply means putting your plant in a bright, sunny room but in a spot where it’s not directly hit by sunlight. East- and west-facing rooms are typically best for high levels of indirect light to get a Christmas cactus to flower well.

If there’s not enough natural light in the spot you’d like your plant to be, then a basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart is the easy answer.

We know that adequate light is vital if a Christmas cactus is to flower, and in the rainforest beneath a dense tree canopy, sunshine is a precious commodity. So Shlumbergera buds lock onto the direction light is coming from – and if you then move the plant, buds will twist towards the changed light source. This sudden environmental shift stresses the plant and buds will likely drop off.

According to recent reports, this phototropism only begins once the flowerbuds start to form a teardrop shape or reach around ¼ inch long, so you have until then to decide exactly where to position your plant for the holidays. Even the slightest rotation causes the plant to waste energy on reorienting buds to the light source, so to get the best possible flower display, many folk draw a small pencil line on the pot and the surface it’s sitting on, so it’s easy to realign if it does get knocked. If you’re using a grow light, mark its position, too, and be careful not to move it.

Once they’ve set their buds, Christmas cacti like a fairly even temperature of around 65-70°F, which happily is the cozy range most of us keep our homes heated to. In their native rainforest where temperatures are normally highly stable, a blast of cold air may herald a life-threatening freeze so can trigger the cactus to immediately enter survival mode. And it's pretty dramatic: if temperatures suddenly dip, Shlumbergera can react by ditching its buds or flowers to conserve energy so it can concentrate on keeping its core alive. This natural response happens just the same in a draft of cold air from a window or when an exterior door is opened and closed.

Ripening fruit produces a harmless gas, ethylene. All fruit that can still ripen after picking – apples, pears, peaches, tomatoes and avocados as well as bananas – produce ethylene, and that’s the exact same gas a Christmas cactus emits when it’s stressed enough to enter survival mode. Understandable, then, that Shlumbergera are incredibly sensitive to this gas, and simply sitting next to a fruit bowl can be enough to trigger Christmas cactus bud drop.

Sources indicate that as this plant naturally evolved to grow in a humid environment, Christmas cacti can really struggle in the dry, heated air of our homes to start with. But place the plant anywhere near a heating vent, radiator or fireplace where the air is continually stripped of moisture, and stems will promptly dehydrate and buds brown, dropping off before the flowers even open. This is one of the most common reasons for a Christmas cactus not flowering as these houseplants are often put on a fireplace mantelpiece or windowsill above a radiator over the holidays.

In a recent development, so, positioning your Shlumbergera well away from any heat source is a must. Take the next step and give your plant the humidity it craves, however, and it will not only flower more profusely but those hydrated blooms will last for longer. Thanks to the regular steam from showers, cooking and kettles, bathrooms and kitchens typically have air that’s moist enough for a Christmas cactus to thrive and, in other rooms, a humidity tray is the solution.

According to recent reports, standing a Christmas cactus on a Bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is ideal, or make your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel pebbles like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot. The plant must sit on the pebbles above the water level so, rather than being drawn up into the potting soil, the water evaporates to add moisture to the air. Another simple way to increase air humidity is to group your Christmas cactus with other houseplants as they’ll form their own microclimate.

If you've been wondering where to put a Christmas cactus, now you know the common places to rule out. It's well worth searching out just the right spot as when a Christmas cactus gets the sunlight, stability and humidity it needs as fall deepens into winter, you’ll be surprised how much more enthusiastically it flowers. Happy holidays!

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.
  • Recent findings suggest that two newly introduced studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth.
  • The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Recent findings suggest that two newly introduced studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

The second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

Recent findings suggest that “Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Industry observers note that parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

Sources indicate that according to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

Industry observers note that A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”.

Industry observers note that it’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

This article was originally published on November 6, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.

Industry observers note that let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen. He’s just that kind of guy — disarmingly affable and sincere and funny. This is a good thing because right now he’s talking about meningitis. Yes, meningitis, that overlooked infection that, you probably didn’t know, kills 1 in 10 who develop it with 1 in 5 having long-term health consequences like brain damage and hearing loss. Also, kids age 16 to 23 have the highest rates of it. And that’s what brings us here with Burrell, a dad of two teens, and a message. In partnership with GSK (for the Ask2BSure campaign) Burrell has teamed up once again with Julie Bowen and a stand-in teen actor (mom and dad are back!) to give awareness and, yes, make jokes.

Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).

So … Why are you, Ty Burrell, America’s dad, talking about meningitis?

Well, it's pretty organic, actually. I have teenage girls, and unfortunately, the most vulnerable population is, actually, I guess, teens to college, 16 to 23. And that's doing large part to the teen lifestyle. My girls play sports, and there's a lot of water bottle swapping. And once you're in college, it's dorm rooms and it's kissing and all of it. And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

In a recent development, but meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. So that's why I'm partnering with GSK on the Ask2BSure campaign to raise awareness about meningococcal disease or meningitis.

To that end, we made a video that we hope is funny, kind of a lighthearted way to educate people and inform people.

In a recent development, it is funny! But I must say as a parent of a 14-year-old, I almost couldn't get the humor because I got afraid.

Yeah, I know. It's a tightrope walk, isn't It?

I happened to have a doctor check in with my 14-year-old this week and I asked them about meningitis. It turns out that I'm two years early. So I'm wondering outside of this PSA, which I think will get people asking doctors, what basic things should parents of teens know.

Well, I would direct them to a healthcare professional in terms of all of the basics. But what I know is that the vaccines available, in terms of strains, A, B, C, W, and Y, but a lot of teens don't have the meningitis B vaccination. And that was true of my 16-year-old. And I did the same thing. When I started to learn more about how serious this was, I had a conversation with our doctor and she hadn't had B yet, so that's now scheduled. And I mean, as far as my knowledge about it, it would be that and really just encouraging people to have a conversation with their doctor about the risks of meningitis and about vaccination, and if that's an option.

Recent findings suggest that it is that simple. I was wondering, I mean, we dads, are always look for a way to make something into a lecture... Is there a way to segue from the meningitis talk or explanation to other necessary talks?

You do have to say it's because you're probably going to be making out with people.

Industry observers note that yeah, totally. I don't know what it's like for you, but I feel like the window in which I actually have any influence for them is three sentences. And I don't know if that's a lack of attention span because of phones or screens or what have you, or it's just time-honored parenting, that you just have the floor for a brief moment before you are tuned out.

“This very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy.”.

And their brains short-circuit.

Totally. And get frustrated fast. It's a lecture. We're now in a lecture. So I don't know about the segueing into a separate topic, but I will say that my wife, luckily, with girls is taking the conversation off of my plate.

Oh great. You can just tell them how dirty dorm rooms are.

Industry observers note that that's the dad's role. So you have two teens now. What's the toughest things you've found about raising them and maybe what's the best?

I think that the really natural want for independence, especially our 16-year-old ... Well, actually both of them, we have a 16 and a 14-year-old, but I think they are both craving more independence and more of their own choices and more of their own time. And yet we're still on the job. We are the ones that have to keep them healthy and safe. And so I feel like, I don't know if you feel this way, but I feel like the challenge is really making them feel heard and seen and giving them as much freedom as I possibly can. And still, which it's hard to do because once they experience some of that freedom, it's very hard for them to then have you say, "But not this thing, that's dangerous," or, "That's unhealthy," or whatever that is.

In a recent development, this is why, and this is very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy. I really want to be their friend, but you really can't ... It's not always an option. It just isn't always an option. A lot of points, you have to actually say, "No, you are going to be mad at me, but this is about health and safety." That's the hardest thing. And then I think added on to that, it's like how do you remain connected to them in a time when they're trying to find their own voice and trying to separate from you really? And I think that's completely natural. They are actually trying to pull away so they can be their own selves, and yet it's really notable, I think, that you stay connected. I got really good advice from this book a long time ago called The Wonder of Girls, and his advice was like, "They're going to be really mean to you, and don't take it personally." He mentioned, "Just stay nearby. Don't take it personally, be nearby." And that's always been in the back of my mind.

Sources indicate that metaphorically, I'm kind of by the doorjamb of the room. Are you thirsty? Everything okay in there? You safe? But yeah, it's not easy.

That's Great. The Go the F*ck to Sleep author just wrote an essay for Fatherly for his latest book Go to the F*ck to College ...

Oh, I didn't know there was a sequel.

In a recent development, it just came out! It should be very pertinent to you. But he talks about one piece advice he got from a friend was all teens are saying, "F*ck you, tuck me in. " And I think it's just a more crude way of saying what you were just saying.

It kind of covers it. I still get requests. My daughter will act like she never wants to see me again, and then I'll hear like, "Are you not tucking me in? " Okay, I guess there's something there still.

So what's the best part of raising a teen? For the preteen parents in our audience, can you give them some hope — and maybe advice?

According to recent reports, I would say the level of nuance in conversation is a real high for me, especially somebody who is interested in comedy. My 16-year-old is pretty stoic. I always think of her as the leading man in a Western or something. She's this person staring off distance, and she's got three words for any answer. But my 14-year-old has always had a strong sense of irony, always, always been funny, and always had a real sense of looking at the world and seeing irony. And as she gets older, her perspective on things, it's pretty remarkable to be around a kid who is starting to see the world and seeing some of the contradictions of the world and some of the things that are unfair, but also just the things that are inherently funny about how seriously we all take ourselves. It's pretty cool. So I think that's one of the great trade-offs is that you end up actually having an intimate relationship with somebody who is really experiencing some of these perspectives for the first time.

Industry observers note that that's great. And then any advice for our younger audience? I mean, as far as parenting advice, but also you were thinking about meningitis, any just really pragmatic pitfalls that you would've done differently?

Sources indicate that I would say if I were going to go back and re-parent, I would say, "Bend, don't break." I would've given them both more of a leash. Leash is a terrible word for kids really, but you know what I mean? More slack in terms of just they're really exploring who they are and letting them really ... I think we did our best with that, but you're so worried about health and safety, that is mental health, physical health. I think that's a major part of why the meningitis, this campaign to talk about it is really key to me because at the very end of the day, that is the bottom line. No matter whether they consider me a friend or not, I do have to keep them safe. And we've already had lots of bugs go through the family from their interactions with other teens, including mono and all kinds of stuff. But if you get meningitis, that's a whole different ballgame.

The Cool Dad’s Guide to Father’s Day

📅 21 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately.
  • But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids.
  • Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

According to recent reports, if you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow).

But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also shows how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”.

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it.".

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

According to recent reports, llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a significant role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas notes, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”.

It has been revealed that tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”.

Sources indicate that tom Llamas and family. Credit: NBC.

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”.

Recent findings suggest that llamas notes he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in Fresh York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”.

This Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”.

From a kid-safe saw (yes, really) to a screen-free telephone “club,” these are the picks blowing up our mom group chats.

It happens like clockwork every fall: Our mom group chats turn into one long stream of links. “Is your kid asking for this, too?” “Is it sold out??” “Ordering now; better safe than sorry!” IYKYK, and if you’re behind, well, we’ve got you.

Our editors pooled our mom group chats to parse through all the convos and conjecture about what our kids want this year, and we came up with a list of kids’ gifts real moms are actually buying (or have already procured and stuffed in a secret hiding place). There’s the landline for kids that you’ve surely been seeing all over your social media feeds, a play saw that won’t cut little fingers, a balance board that’s sneaky good for everyone in the house, and much more. There’s guaranteed to be something for every kind of kid on this list.

Keep scrolling for the gifts every mom we know is talking about.

For the baby or toddler on your holiday list, a Lovevery Play Kit is genuinely one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each kit is developmentally designed by experts for a specific age and stage, so every single toy inside has a real purpose and actually supports what that child’s brain is working on right now. The Free Spirit Kit is designed for older toddlers exploring independence, creativity, and imaginative play, and it comes with everything from open-ended building materials to pretend play pieces that grow with them well beyond the holiday season. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

The Sticki Rolls capsule series has absolutely taken over my daughter’s friend group, so she will lose her mind when she sees Series 3 under the tree. Each roll is a peel-and-stick experience that reveals collectible band stickers inside, and the trading, collecting, and comparing with friends has become a whole social event in itself. They are the kind of small, inexpensive gift that delivers an enormous reaction, which is the ideal holiday gift math. It’s the perfect stocking stuffer or add-on for any kid who is deep in the sticker and collectible era right now! — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, this is the holiday gift that every parent who is trying to delay handing their kid a smartphone needs to know about. The Tin Can is a Wi-Fi landline designed specifically for kids, with no screen, no apps, no social media, no browser, and no strangers getting through. You control the approved contact list from the app, kids can call friends and family with real voice calls, and there is even a free Can-to-Can proposal so two Tin Can kids can call each other for free with no subscription required. My daughter loves it and I love that she gets the independence of being able to call her people without me handing over the entire internet to do it. — Katie Garrity.

This is such an ideal holiday toy for me! It's physical but can be done inside, it's not made of plastic, it doesn't have noise or lights, and... I can use it too after the kids go to bed. Also you don't have to wrap it. Really, can you ask for anything more? — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

In a recent development, the Melissa & Doug Cheery Lane House is the kind of gift that becomes the centerpiece of playtime for years — it is a beautifully detailed wooden dollhouse play set with colorful, cheerful design that sparks hours of open-ended storytelling and creative play without a single battery or screen required. Melissa & Doug has been the gold standard in wooden toys and imaginative play for decades, and this set delivers on every bit of that quality and craftsmanship. — Katie Garrity.

The Noodoll Ricespud Hot Potato is a tiny, perfectly rendered little potato plush that is so absurd and so cute at the same time that it is genuinely impossible not to love it. It is soft, squishy, palm-sized, and has the most deadpan little potato face that somehow communicates everything. It’s the kind of completely unhinged gift that costs almost nothing, takes up zero space in a stocking, and becomes the most talked-about thing under the tree because nobody expected a potato and yet here we all are. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, the ChompSaw is the coolest thing I have seen for kids who want to actually make things. It is a real, functional saw designed specifically for children with a safety guard that prevents the blade from cutting skin but still cuts wood, foam, and cardboard perfectly, which means she gets the genuine satisfaction of building and creating without me hovering anxiously over every cut. It’s designed for kids 4 and up, requires zero power tools or adult intervention once they gets the hang of it, and the independent building projects it unlocks are genuinely impressive. — Katie Garrity.

I love this toy because it combines two really common kid interests: building things and dinosaurs. I got this set for my twin neice and nephew and they have gotten so much (QUIET, SOLO) play time from this set. This set allows you to make three different dinosauts — T-rex, pterodactyl, brontosaurus — and they make them over and over again. It's hands-on and it uses their brains, I couldn't ask for more. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that my daughter has been asking to learn to sew and this is the perfect place to start. The Hug is a beginner-friendly kids’ sewing machine that uses yarn instead of thread, making it safe, easy, and genuinely manageable for little hands without the frustration of rethreading a needle every five minutes. It has a built-in safety finger guard, LED lighting, and comes with a full sewing kit so she can start creating immediately right out of the box. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I have a soccer obsessed kid; specifically, he wants to play goalie all the time. We practice every. Single. Day. And he always wants more time and more kicks to block. This soccer launcher has been so fun. It will fire on a five-second timer or if you clap three times, and you can adjust the height it debuts at too. It's a great "big" gift for the soccer loving kid in your life. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

K-Pop and cool fashion dolls in the same box is basically a guaranteed win. The K-Pop Demon Hunters 3-pack features three fully styled dolls with incredible detail in their outfits, accessories, and overall aesthetic that feels genuinely fresh and different from anything else in the doll aisle right now. Each doll has her own distinct look and personality, and the whole set comes with the kind of intricate styling details that a kid who loves fashion, music, and K-Pop culture will absolutely obsess over. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that magnetic tiles are one of those gifts that never get old, and a 132-piece set is the kind of haul that opens up a whole fresh level of what they can build. The Sunny Auntie tiles are compatible with other major magnetic tile brands so they can add to an existing collection, the pieces are thick, sturdy, and safe with rounded edges and no sharp corners, and the variety of shapes in the set means endless architectural possibilities from simple towers to elaborate castles and everything in between. — Katie Garrity.

This collab between Melissa & Doug and the iconic Van Leeuwen Ice Cream is the most delightful play set, and the little ones on your holiday list are going to absolutely love it! It is a fully detailed pretend play ice cream counter inspired by Van Leeuwen’s gorgeous aesthetic, complete with scoopable play ice cream, cones, toppings, and all the tools needed for the most imaginative scoop shop experience. — Katie Garrity.

If you have been anywhere near a toy store, a bookstore, or the internet in the last year you already know that Jellycat has completely taken over, and this little Scottie Dog in his cozy winter jumper is exactly why. The softness is genuinely unmatched, the details are ridiculously charming, and every single Jellycat somehow manages to have more personality than a stuffed animal has any right to. My daughter because she has been asking for a Jellycat, and a dog in a tiny Christmas sweater felt like the obvious and correct choice. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, my 8-year-old niece loved this pen creation station. Craft kits feel like they're back in a massive way this year, and I love that this one is fun during the making and leaves you with usable pens she can take to school, and a fun little storage locker for her desk in her room. It's just little girl gift gold. — Katie McPherson.

According to recent reports, knuffle Bunny is a full cultural moment right now, and if your kid has read Mo Willems’ beloved picture book series, getting the actual official stuffed animal is going to completely send them. The Gund version is beautifully made with that signature floppy, scrappy, well-loved look that matches the book illustrations perfectly, and the softness is exactly what you want from a toy that is going to become a forever comfort companion. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, the combination of Bluey and the Scribble Scrubbie concept is genuinely my daughter’s two favorite hobbies all in one. The Scribble Scrubbie pets are washable toy figures that kids can color with markers, scrub clean, and color all over again, which means the creative play never runs out. The Bluey version gives you Bluey and Bingo to color and decorate, which is going to be an absolutely unhinged amount of fun for any kid obsessed with the show. — Katie Garrity.

For the kid who already has a Nugget and is completely obsessed with Minecraft, this cover set is going to make the holidays. The Minecraft collab brings the iconic blocky aesthetic to the covers in a way that is genuinely cool and immediately recognizable to any fan. It transforms an already beloved piece of furniture into the ultimate Minecraft hangout zone without any fresh hardware required, just swap the covers and watch your kid completely lose their mind. — Katie Garrity.

We've tried a few different audio players over the years and the Yoto is the one that has really stuck for my son. He uses it every night to listen to a story while he drifts off, and he looks forward to the Yoto Daily podcast with Jake too. This generation of Yoto has so many features I love, from the built-in night light (no more traveling with both!), to the latest green button on the side that makes it easy to toggle through favorite stories without carrying along their cards. This is a fabulous gift idea that'll truly be used and loved for many years to come (ours has been THROWN many times during toddler tantrums and still works like a dream). — Katie McPherson.

This is a craft kit and a fidget toy in one, which is basically the dream combo for a kid who can’t sit still. The kit comes with 101 scented squishy beads in flower, heart, round, and star shapes, plus five reusable elastic bracelets and a beading needle, so my daughter can make a bracelet, squish it, take it apart, and start over. It’s a screen-free gift that keeps her hands busy for hours, and I’m not above admitting I’ll probably end up making a bracelet too! — Katie Garrity.

These are just the cutest overalls that remind me of what I wore when I was a kid. They're designed by Sergio Hudson, who did a special collaboration with Osh Kosh this winter. I love the pop of color, I love the stripes, I love it all. And I know your kid will, too. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

This is the gift that keeps my daughter happily occupied without a screen in sight, and the starter set means there’s no scrambling to figure out what else you need. You just set a Tonie character on top of the box and it plays stories, songs, and adventures, and it’s simple enough that she runs the whole thing herself. It’s become part of our daily routine, and it’s the kind of present kids keep reaching for long after the wrapping paper is gone! — Katie Garrity.

The “more is more” customizing trend is real in our house, and these let my daughter decorate everything she owns without a single bottle of glue. Each pack has 15 glossy, 3D resin charms in pink kawaii creatures, sweet treats, and whimsical icons that peel off the backing and stick to anything flat, like her phone case, journal, or water bottle. It’s a small, inexpensive gift that gets a big reaction, and I fully expect to find a tiny charm stuck to something I own by January. — Katie Garrity.

This upcoming set from Magna-Tiles takes everything my daughter loves about building with Magna-Tiles and adds ball runs, which means she gets to engineer a track and then immediately test whether it works. The set has 78 magnetic pieces plus two racing balls, including a trapdoor, a slide, and curved and short rails, so she can build multi-level raceways with tight turns and significant drops. It works with any Magna-Tiles she already owns, and it’s a screen-free gift that teaches cause and effect while she thinks she’s just playing. — Katie Garrity.

There’s SNOW much to love about this limited-edition Snoopy purse, which is designed to look like a mini puffer coat with a quilted detail and a chain strap. It comes in a pretty Swiss blue, closes with a magnetic snap, and is part of Janie and Jack’s winter PEANUTS collection, so it’s guaranteed to make her whole cozy-weather outfit feel complete. It’s small and special enough to fit all her tiny treasures! — Katie Garrity.

I've had my eye on the Nex for a long time, and I wish I'd gotten one sooner! We love gaming as a family and it makes me so happy to have the Nex on the mantle for rainy or cold days when it's zero fun to be outside, but we neeeeed to move around and burn energy. It's gaming with way less guilt and feels like a family activity we all look forward to. And yeah, Fruit Ninja is just way more fun when you're karate chopping with your whole chest rather than getting finger burn swiping like crazy. — Katie McPherson.

I got this set for my upcoming niece, and I still cannot get over how perfect it is! It’s soft and airy, thanks to the 100% cotton gauze, and that hand-drawn tulip print? Stahhhp, it’s so charming. It’s a good thing my kids are no longer little or I would literally be buying up every single thing on this site. I think this would make the sweetest gift for any little girl in your life. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

This fresh board game has everything I like: easy rules, really beautiful design, and short game play (around a half-hour). I also love 2-player games that I can either play with one kid or with my partner. The premise is very simple: build a 3D volcano with certain features before your opponent does. I love that this can be very simple or very strategic — there's also an expansion set that bring the game up to 4 players. — Sarah Aswell.

For the little racer who’s obsessed with Mario Kart, this officially licensed slot car set brings the game to the living room floor, with Mario and Yoshi going head to head on a 9-foot track with a built-in lap counter to crown the winner. It’s made for kids ages 3 and up and gives two players a screen-free way to duke it out, which is the kind of gift that gets pulled out over and over. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, if you have a kid who refuses to come inside until her fingers are numb, this is the snowsuit that lets her stay out there, because it’s waterproof and breathable, so she stays dry whether she’s sledding, skiing, or face-planting into a snowbank. It’s built with real snowsport details, including several pockets and adjustability, so it can keep up with a growing kid through the whole winter. It's a splurge, but it’s the one piece of winter gear that makes getting her out the door a lot less of a battle. — Katie Garrity.

Anyone else have a Grinch-obsessed child? The Grinch with a light-up heart is basically the holiday plush equivalent of a happy ending, and she already quotes the movie every December. It’s an 18-inch, soft and fuzzy Grinch with a glowing heart on his chest, which makes it a great cuddle buddy and a night-time companion all season. Made for ages 2 and up, it’s the kind of gift that instantly becomes a holiday tradition (and gets a spot on the couch until New Year’s). — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, now, this a video game I can say yes to without a second thought, with Bluey and Bingo finding Dad’s old camera and snapping photos around the show’s famous spots, then saving everything in a scrapbook she can decorate with stickers. It has local co-op so a second player can join in and strike a pose, plus no in-game purchases and no online play, which is the kind of kid-friendly setup parents love. The Deluxe Edition adds the Here Come the Grannies bonus content, extra dress-up items, and a digital art book, and the “For Real Life” activity ideas even get her playing away from the screen. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, OK so... I want one of these, too. My two tween girls are VERY into fidget toys and squishies, so we have a lot in my house. My favorite one to steal is this butter block. It's adorable on my desk and great to squeeze during meetings and phone calls. But also great for the kids they're meant for. And fits in a stocking! — Sarah Aswell.

For the toddler in your life who already knows every word to Ms. Rachel’s songs, this Yoto card puts the whole debut album on a screen-free player, with all 23 tracks, including “Icky Sticky Bubblegum,” “I Love a Rainbow,” “Significant Feelings,” and a few classics like “The Wheels on the Bus.” Kids just pop the card into a Yoto Player or Yoto Mini to hear it, which means a dance party can happen without anyone handing over a phone. It’s $14.99, made for ages 1 and up, and the card debuts Nov. 12, so it’s available to preorder now, which makes it a perfect stocking stuffer for any family that already has a Yoto. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that for the kid on your list who’s obsessed with Star Wars, this 13-inch remote control walker is basically a movie scene they can drive around the living room, with a Mandalorian and Grogu figure riding in the cockpit. It really walks, runs, and turns with a 2.4 GHz remote, and it comes loaded with LED lights, laser cannon sounds, and real Star Wars audio clips, so every trip across the floor feels like a battle. It’s made for ages 8 and up and is a Walmart exclusive, and honestly the walker looks cool enough on a shelf that parents will be tempted to play too. — Katie Garrity.

My 11-year-old kid is so hard to buy presents for. She's kind of not into toys anymore, but she's not ready to go over to the realm of all clothes and self-care and novels yet. Well... when I saw this Chia Pet bison... I know that she would have at least one thing under the tree that she absolutely loved. I love that this has a bit of a "toy" feel, but it's also cool room decor. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, these 14-inch dolls are incredily cute and well-made. I love that the dolls look like actual normal girls without exaggerated or sexualized features and I love that the price point adds a good option for families that can't drop three digits for an American Girl Dolls. There are also lots of great accessories available, also at reasonable prices! — Sarah Aswell.

I genuinely would put these on and wear them myself if I could, but I suppose I’ll just have to settle for watching my niece romp around in them. I love that these are fully waterpoof but also lightweight and flexible enough that kids don’t feel like they’re walking around wearing cinder blocks. Another great feature is the grippy outsole to help keep little ones from slipping while they’re exploring on wet ground. And they’re made from natural rubber, so totally non-toxic! — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that clickeez are tiny character keycaps that click and clack like a real mechanical keyboard, and the Series 3 Bubble Pops theme has a softer, quieter click that’s almost as satisfying as the surprise of seeing which ones you get. The Mega Pack comes with a keyboard-shaped case and 12 characters to display and swap in and out, plus there are 70+ characters to hunt for, including rare surprises, so she can build a collection one click at a time. It’s made for ages 6 and up and is a great screen-free gift for any kid who loves to collect (and click)! — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, the details in this LEGO build are amazing, from the chain-driven V* engine compressor to the functional steering and suspension. Honestly, I got this car for my (grown, adult) brother and a different, simpler Fast and Furious car for my nephew to build along side him. I love how many brain-building, screenless hours of fun these sets provide — and then you can watch the movie after. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that I mean, the title really explains everything. This shoots farts at people. I fully admit that I bought this for my brother's children and not for mine, and they played with it for *hours*. There was so much laughter, and honestly, the smell is not that bad for the adults in the room (although we did kick them outside). I think they ran more than when they play sports. — Sarah Aswell.

Is there anything cuter than a denim jacket on a child? No there is not. Enter this adorable teddy fleece-lined jacket that you just know your kid will love. It's cozy, classic and totally show-stopping. — Kate Auletta.

In a recent development, every mom knows that it’s the absolute worst when your little one is feeling under the weather... and it can especially wreak havoc on sleep. Kids will love getting it as a gift, but Mom might love it even more. — Julie Sprankles.

35 Back-To-School Sports Gear Essentials Every Young Athlete Needs

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.
  • Sources indicate that back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has.
  • According to recent reports, most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

Sources indicate that back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

According to recent reports, most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and substantial enough to get them through practice.

Industry observers note that the 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

It has been revealed that some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

This variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

Recent findings suggest that some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. A protein bar is useful before practice, after practice, or between games, but check school rules and allergens before tossing one into a team bag.

Recent findings suggest that this 10-count variety pack has flavors built around chocolate, peanut butter, blueberry, fruit, and nuts. The bars are gluten-free, made with simple ingredients, and have 12 grams of protein per bar, but some contain common allergens including eggs, peanuts, almonds, and cashews.

Fall sports still mean sun exposure. A sweat-resistant sunscreen belongs in every sports bag, especially for after-school practices, weekend tournaments and kids who swear they “don’t burn.”.

This sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

In a recent development, this has a spacious main compartment for school and practice gear, plus a ventilated shoe compartment to keep wet sneakers or cleats away from clean clothes and tech. The water-resistant base is the quiet win here, because locker room floors, wet fields, and rainy parking lots are not kind to regular backpacks.

In a recent development, wet socks, damp towels, and postpractice clothes should not touch anything clean. A wet-dry bag keeps the gross stuff contained until someone remembers laundry exists.

According to recent reports, these bags are technically built for diapers, swimsuits, and day care messes, which is exactly why it works for youth sports. The 12.5-by-16-inch size, washable fabric, heat-sealed seams, and leak-resistant design make it useful for wet socks, damp towels, and gear you do not want touching anything else.

Industry observers note that cotton is fine until it turns into a wet dish towel with sleeves. A moisture-wicking shirt helps kids stay more comfortable through practice, conditioning, and the ride home.

Sources indicate that the quick-drying fabric wicks sweat and dries fast, which is the whole point of a practice shirt. It is soft enough for school or general wear too, so it does not become another piece of gear that only gets used once a week.

In a recent development, every young athlete needs shorts that can handle sweat, dirt, turf, and repeated washing. They should be light, easy to move in, and not so expensive that losing one pair becomes a family event.

#33152. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

📅 15 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2066 w)
